query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an ultrathin alumina (Al2O3) coating via atomic layer deposition (ALD) on the surface of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will significantly improve its oxidation resistance at high temperature without degrading its inherent mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but with poor oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Depositing an ultrathin (e.g., ~10 nm) dense alumina (Al2O3) coating by atomic layer deposition.
generation.conditions: Expose coated samples to 1 atm O2 at 1000 °C for 100 hours. After exposure, assess mechanical performance under strain rates ranging from 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻² s⁻¹, and check that room-temperature tensile ductility remains within 8–16% and high-temperature yield strength stays between 163–530 MPa.
generation.structural_mediator: The uniform, conformal alumina layer acts as a diffusion barrier, preventing oxygen ingress into the bulk alloy.
generation.mechanism: The ALD-deposited alumina forms a protective, thermodynamically stable oxide scale that retards oxidation at elevated temperatures, thereby preserving the microstructure and mechanical integrity of the underlying alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: The intervention will lead to a marked reduction in oxygen-induced degradation (e.g., lower mass gain during oxidation testing) while maintaining comparable room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength relative to untreated casting.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, which suffers from significant oxygen ingress and subsequent degradation of mechanical properties during high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: Temperature: 1000 °C; Atmosphere: 1 atm O2; Exposure time: 100 hours; Mechanical loading: strain rates of 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.uncertainty: Long-term adhesion and durability of the ultrathin alumina coating under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading remain uncertain and may require further evaluation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of cast HfNbTaTiZr samples: one group receives the ~10 nm alumina coating via ALD, and the other remains untreated. Expose both groups to 1 atm O2 at 1000 °C for 100 hours. Afterwards, measure mass gain, characterize the surface oxidation (via microscopy and oxygen depth profiling), and perform mechanical tests to assess room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength under strain rates of 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻² s⁻¹.
measurements: Mass gain (mg/cm²) to assess oxidation extent
Surface microscopy and depth profiling to evaluate oxide scale integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (mass gain and oxygen penetration similar to untreated samples) or if the mechanical properties (tensile ductility and yield strength) fall outside the acceptable ranges (8–16% ductility, 163–530 MPa strength) compared to the untreated alloy, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As the temperature capability of modern Ni- based superalloys has reached its limit for gas turbine engine applications, materials scientists are searching for new materials with higher temperature capabilities. Recently, “High-Entropy Alloy (HEA)” [1] , [2] has been proposed as a new strategy for alloy design with a wide composition space. Other names such as “compositionally complex alloys (CCAs)” has also been given to this class of alloy containing multiple phases [3] . Nevertheless, the alloy design strategy of HEA/CCA shows great promise for exploring new alloy systems. RHEA was first proposed by Senkov et al . [4] as an attempt to create new alloy systems for high temperature applications beyond superalloys. By combining refractory elements such as W, Mo, Ta, Nb, Hf, …etc. in equi- or near equi-molar ratios, several RHEAs with promising mechanical properties have been reported [5] – [7] . However, oxidation resistance is crucial since it could lead to severe degradation in mechanical properties. occupying_moves.technique: atomic layer deposition of an ultrathin alumina (Al2O3) coating
occupying_moves.conditions: Testing at 1000 °C in an oxygen‐rich atmosphere (1 atm O2) for a controlled exposure time (e.g., 100 hours) while maintaining strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹ to verify retention of 8–16% room‐temperature tensile ductility and similar high‐temperature yield strength levels.

chosen.technique: atomic layer deposition of an ultrathin alumina (Al2O3) coating
chosen.conditions: Expose the coated HfNbTaTiZr alloy to 1 atm O2 at 1000 °C for 100 hours, and then assess mechanical performance under strain rates ranging from 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻² s⁻¹ to confirm that tensile ductility (8–16% at room temperature) and yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C) remain unaffected.
chosen.why: This intervention directly addresses the identified performance limitation by creating a dense, protective oxide layer that inhibits oxygen ingress without altering the bulk alloy properties. Atomic layer deposition is a standard and precise technique in materials science for ensuring uniform, ultrathin coatings, and similar approaches have been successfully employed in refractory and high-temperature alloys to improve oxidation resistance.
